title: Weight Updates as Activation Shifts
one_liner: Activation steering (tweaking internal states without changing weights) does the same job as weight-updating, and you can use this to adapt models far more efficiently.
lead: When you want to teach a pretrained model a new task, you normally adjust its weights (the knobs that control its behavior). But there is a cheaper way: you can intercept the numbers flowing inside the model at certain points and nudge them without touching the weights at all, because nudging those internal numbers at the right spot produces the same effect as weight adjustment. This paper proves this and tells you exactly where to nudge for best results.

paras: When a large pretrained model lands on your task, fine-tuning it by adjusting all its weights works but is expensive (storing and computing updates for millions of numbers). A shortcut: intercept the numbers flowing inside the model between layers and nudge just those numbers, leaving weights untouched. We call this steering.

The catch: nobody knew where to intercept or how to nudge. Engineers tried different spots (early layers, middle layers, outputs) and different nudge types and picked the one that seemed to work best on their specific task. This works but is slow and unreliable. You end up with a pile of task-specific recipes with no rhyme or reason.

callout.html: Activation steering (intercepting and nudging internal states) can do exactly what weight-updating does, and here is the math to find where to nudge.

panels.title: 3. The paper's insight
panels.caption: A nudge at the right spot produces identical effect to weight update. They are twins.

panels.title: 4. Where to nudge
panels.viz_args: Post-block output is the sweet spot.
panels.caption: The math shows: intercept after each layer for best steering power.

panels.title: 5. Joint steering

steps.b: Map activation nudges to weight space
steps.text: A small change to internal states (activations) between layers produces a predictable change in weights.
The post-block output (after the layer processes information) is where a nudge has the most steering power.
Instead of updating weights, train to nudge internal numbers at the right spot. 0.04% of the numbers, same accuracy.
Weight updates and activation nudges do different jobs; training both together beats either alone.
Show that post-block steering recovers the same task performance as full fine-tuning.

paras: Instead of adjusting weights (the model's permanent knobs), the paper adjusts internal numbers: the flowing data that represent the model's thought at each step. Specifically, it nudges the output after each layer (where a layer is a processing step in the model; after the layer combines input data with weights and does some math). By changing these internal numbers, the model adapts to a new task without retraining its weights.
object.object: where to nudge and how much

hidden.name: how much a nudge at each location changes the task output
paras: The paper measures a hidden quantity: the sensitivity of the model's task performance to nudges at each layer. At some spots (like early layers), nudging has almost no effect on the final answer. At other spots (post-block outputs), a small nudge radically changes what the model predicts. This sensitivity is the 'steering power': how much steering authority you have at that spot. A nudge at post-block is like steering a steering wheel; a nudge at an early layer is like trying to steer by tweaking a pebble in the road.

The paper derives this by comparing internal nudges to weight updates mathematically. It asks: if I nudge internal numbers at layer L, what weights would produce the same effect? By answering that, it can see which layers are most effective for steering.

heat.caption: Darker means more steering power. Post-block (highlighted) is the sweet spot.

reads.html: Some layers are like steering a small car on ice (nudges barely matter); post-block is like steering on pavement (nudges have huge effect).
First-order derivative of task loss with respect to activations at layer L; highest at post-block outputs.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the weight-activation bridge
paras: Here is the core insight. When you fine-tune by updating weights, you are computing how to shift each weight so the model predicts correctly on the new task. The paper shows: nudging internal numbers at the post-block output is mathematically equivalent to shifting weights upstream. Specifically, if you nudge the internal numbers by amount delta at layer L, it is the same as shifting the weights in layer L by an amount that depends on delta and the incoming signal. This is a first-order equivalence: at small nudges, they are twins.

Why does this work? Because internal numbers are the bottleneck where all information flows between layers. The output of a block is the summary of what that block learned to compute. By nudging that summary, you redirect the model's reasoning downstream without needing to retrain. Early layers (where the model detects low-level patterns) are less useful for steering because nudging them is far removed from the final prediction, so the effect fades as it flows downstream; post-block is optimal because it is the last chance to redirect before the prediction, so your nudge has maximum effect on the final answer.

math.words: activation nudge effect equals weight change in upstream layer times incoming signal
symbols: the nudge we apply to activations at layer L

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Imagine a layer with 4 input numbers [2, 3, 1, 2] and weights arranged in a 4-by-4 grid.
To produce the effect of nudging internal numbers by [0.5, 0, 0, 0], the math shows you need weight shifts that when multiplied by [2, 3, 1, 2] give [0.5, 0, 0, 0].
So: a nudge to a post-block internal number is exactly like adjusting weights to redirect the signal. Small nudges, same effect, training only 0.04% of weights.

math.note: When internal nudges and weight updates are equivalent, steering at post-block is both theoretically justified and highly effective.

charts.title: Full fine-tuning
charts.note: Gold standard: adjust all weights, takes time, perfect accuracy.

charts.title: Post-block steering only
charts.note: Post-block steering: adjust 0.04% of weights, nearly as accurate, drastically faster, because the math shows post-block nudges have maximal effect on the final prediction.

items.html: If you nudge early layers, the effect is drowned out by downstream computation. The model ignores your nudge because it is too far from the output. Solution: use post-block outputs.

Activation steering is a first-order equivalence, meaning it works for small nudges. Large nudges violate the math and the model may crash or output garbage. Solution: train the nudge size, do not hardcode it.

If you train internal nudges only (no weight updates), the model overfits to the one task. Adding a little weight updating makes it generalize better, because weight updates spread the learning across the whole model while nudges concentrate the steering at one point. Solution: combine weight and internal-number training.
Post-block steering with moderate nudges, trained end-to-end, achieves within 0.2%-0.9% accuracy of full fine-tuning while training only 0.04% of weights.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny model on a simple task (e.g., a small language model on sentiment classification). First, fine-tune it fully by adjusting all weights (baseline). Second, freeze weights and train only post-block internal-number nudges (activation steering). Third, train both simultaneously (joint adaptation). Compare accuracy on a held-out test set. The demo should show: (1) steering alone gets within a few percentage points of full fine-tuning, because post-block is where nudges have the most effect; (2) post-block is better than middle layers, because early layers' effects are diluted by downstream computation; (3) joint adaptation beats either alone, because weight shifts and internal nudges do complementary jobs (weights adjust the global tendency, nudges make fine corrections).
demo.metric_eq: accuracy_gap = accuracy_finetuned - accuracy_steered; should be less than 1%
demo.closing: If post-block steering recovers nearly all accuracy using 0.04% of weights, the equivalence is real.
